questions.title: How can an FBI investigation count as an "enforcement proceeding" under FOIA Exemption 7(A) if no charges have been filed?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the court's statement that ongoing criminal investigations themselves can qualify as "enforcement proceedings" for purposes of Exemption 7(A). I thought an enforcement proceeding meant something more formal, like an indictment, trial, or at least an administrative adjudication. Here, the FBI seems to have relied largely on declarations saying the investigation was still ongoing. Why is that enough under D.C. Circuit precedent, and what limits are there to stop agencies from calling any open-ended investigation a pending proceeding?

questions.title: What does it mean for records to be "compiled for law enforcement purposes" when the FBI is also dealing with national security matters?
questions.question_body: The opinion says the FBI gets some deference because it is a law-enforcement agency, but it still has to show a "rational nexus" between the investigation and a law-enforcement duty, plus a connection to a possible security risk or violation of law. I'm having trouble understanding how demanding that test really is in practice. If the investigation involves terrorism or national security, does that automatically satisfy the "law enforcement purposes" requirement, or does the agency still need to tie the file to a specific possible violation of federal law?

questions.title: Why did the court treat the newer Bender declaration as an "update" instead of requiring a full fresh showing for Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: The district court denied summary judgment without prejudice because the earlier Hardy declarations might have become stale. Then the FBI came back with a pretty short Bender declaration saying the investigation remained ongoing, plus a sealed ex parte submission. On appeal, Farahi argued that this was too conclusory. I'm confused about why the D.C. Circuit didn't require the FBI to fully re-establish the existence of pending or reasonably anticipated proceedings as of 2023, instead of letting it rely on the earlier Hardy declarations plus a brief update.

questions.title: When are ex parte and sealed declarations allowed in FOIA cases, and does failing to object waive challenges to them?
questions.question_body: A lot of the court's reasoning seems to depend on sealed ex parte declarations that the requester could not see. I understand the practical reason for that in sensitive cases, but I'm not sure about the procedural rules. Is it generally acceptable in FOIA litigation for the government to make key showings ex parte, especially on issues like Exemption 7(A) and segregability? Also, the opinion says Farahi did not oppose the district court's acceptance of ex parte declarations, so he could not later challenge reliance on them. Is that a true waiver/forfeiture rule, and how specific would an objection have needed to be?

questions.title: How can an agency satisfy FOIA's segregability requirement when it withholds almost an entire investigative file?
questions.question_body: The FBI found over 10,000 pages and 80 CDs, disclosed some material, and withheld most of the rest. Farahi argued that there had to be at least some non-exempt information buried in a file that large. The court responded that isolated words or phrases are not necessarily "reasonably segregable" if they are interspersed line-by-line and don't convey meaningful information. I'm struggling with how courts determine what counts as a "reasonably segregable portion" versus meaningless fragments. At what point does withholding nearly everything become inconsistent with FOIA's general disclosure rule?

questions.title: Why did the court say Farahi forfeited his challenge to the FBI's document categories?
questions.question_body: The opinion briefly mentions that when an agency withholds records by category, the categories must be sufficiently distinct for the court to test whether the exemptions were properly applied. But then it says Farahi forfeited this argument because he did not specifically explain why the FBI's categories were overbroad. What exactly would a FOIA plaintiff need to argue to preserve this kind of issue on appeal? Is a general objection that the categories are too vague not enough?

questions.title: How much deference do courts really give the FBI in Exemption 7(A) cases involving terrorism or national security?
questions.question_body: The court repeatedly emphasizes deference to the FBI as a law-enforcement agency, and says that deference is especially appropriate where national security is implicated. I'm trying to understand the doctrinal significance of that. Does this deference affect only how the court reads the agency's declarations, or does it effectively lower the government's burden of proof? In other words, if the case did not involve terrorism-related allegations, would the same public declarations have been viewed as too conclusory?
